title: "paypal" with one Cyrillic letter looks identical and NFKC does not catch it
assumption: Two strings that render identically are either literally equal, or become equal after Unicode normalization.

input.display: "payp\u0430l" (Cyrillic \u0430, CYRILLIC SMALL LETTER A, in place of the fourth letter) vs "paypal"
input.description: An impersonation username, support-ticket display name, or phishing domain label built by swapping one Latin letter for a visually identical letter from another script.

what_goes_wrong: The spoofed string has the same length as the real word and looks the same in most fonts, but == and a database UNIQUE constraint treat it as a different value, and NFKC normalization leaves it unchanged, so it does not merge with the real spelling.
why: Unicode gives Cyrillic \u0430 and Latin "a" separate code points because they are different letters in different scripts, even though most fonts draw them the same; UTS #39's confusables data lists exactly this kind of pair. Normalization (NFC, NFKC) only replaces a character with an equivalent that Unicode's decomposition data declares, such as a ligature, a fullwidth form or a superscript; there is no such mapping from Cyrillic \u0430 to Latin a, so NFKC leaves the lookalike in place. UTS #39 provides the checks that catch it: comparing "skeletons" built from confusables.txt (which maps \u0430 to a), or mixed-script detection, which flags a single word that mixes Latin and Cyrillic letters.

repros.code:
import unicodedata
a = "paypal"
b = "payp\u0430l"
print(a == b, len(a), len(b))
print(unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", a) == unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", b))
print([hex(ord(c)) for c in b])

fix: For security-sensitive comparisons (brand names, support impersonation, domain labels), run Unicode's confusables skeleton algorithm (UTS #39) in addition to normalization, or restrict the field to a single script/ASCII where the context allows it, rather than trusting that normalization catches lookalikes.

sources.title: UTS #39: Unicode Security Mechanisms, Confusable Detection

test_cases.note: A confusable-aware key for impersonation checks (for example the UTS #39 skeleton) should map both strings to the same key. Plain equality and NFKC both say they differ, which is the gap.
